presentingComplaint: Transient loss of consciousness while climbing stairs, preceded by chest tightness and breathlessness.
history: A 68-year-old man with Child-Pugh B alcohol-related cirrhosis (abstinent 2 years, on spironolactone and propranolol for varices) presents after collapsing during exertion. Over the past 4 months he has had progressive exertional dyspnoea and central chest tightness on walking uphill, and two prior near-syncopal episodes on exertion. Today he blacked out momentarily while climbing a flight of stairs, with rapid full recovery and no post-ictal confusion, tongue-biting or incontinence. His family attributed his fatigue and ankle swelling to 'his liver', which delayed presentation. He denies palpitations preceding the event. No fever. The overlap of ascites, low-grade jaundice and a soft systolic murmur previously misattributed to a hyperdynamic cirrhotic circulation had obscured the valvular picture.
examination: Alert, GCS 15, mildly icteric. Slow-rising, low-volume carotid pulse with narrow pulse pressure. Apex beat non-displaced, heaving. Harsh late-peaking ejection systolic murmur loudest at the right upper sternal edge radiating to both carotids, with soft/absent A2. Bibasal fine crackles and mild bilateral ankle oedema. Abdomen distended with shifting dullness (moderate ascites), non-tender; no asterixis, no encephalopathy. Chest pain reproduced only on exertion, not on palpation.

labs.note: Mild hs-troponin elevation attributed to demand ischaemia/LVH; no dynamic rise. Coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia reflect cirrhosis and complicate any intervention.

imaging: CXR: mild cardiomegaly with upper-lobe venous diversion; calcified aortic valve; no acute consolidation. ECG: sinus rhythm with LVH by voltage and lateral strain; no acute ST-elevation or dynamic ischaemic change. Transthoracic echocardiography: heavily calcified trileaflet aortic valve with severely restricted opening, peak velocity 4.6 m/s, mean gradient 52 mmHg, aortic valve area 0.7 cm2, preserved LVEF 55% with concentric LVH — severe aortic stenosis.
microbiology: Not indicated; afebrile, no infective focus. Blood cultures not required unless endocarditis suspected.
differentialDiagnoses: Severe aortic stenosis with exertional (effort) syncope
Arrhythmic syncope (paroxysmal AF or heart block)
finalDiagnosis: Severe calcific aortic stenosis presenting with exertional syncope and angina, in a patient with alcohol-related cirrhosis complicating management.
citations: ACC/AHA — Management of Valvular Heart Disease — 2020
ESC/EACTS — Guidelines for the Management of Valvular Heart Disease — 2021
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e — Valvular Heart Disease (Aortic Stenosis)
stewardship: Not applicable — non-infective valvular emergency. No antimicrobials indicated. Focus is on echocardiographic confirmation of severe AS, symptom-driven urgency (syncope + angina signal a poor prognosis without intervention), and multidisciplinary Heart Team + hepatology assessment. Cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, thrombocytopenia, INR 1.5) raises surgical/procedural risk and favours careful evaluation for TAVI versus SAVR; avoid volume depletion, nitrates and afterload-reducing agents that can precipitate hypotension in fixed obstruction.
contraindications: Avoid nitrates and other vasodilators/afterload reducers — can cause profound hypotension and syncope in fixed outflow obstruction
Avoid aggressive diuresis/preload reduction — preload-dependent LV can decompensate
Caution with any procedure given cirrhotic coagulopathy (INR 1.5) and thrombocytopenia (platelets 92)
Avoid beta-blocker up-titration that may impair cardiac output in severe AS
edgeCases: Cirrhotic hyperdynamic circulation and ascites can mask or mimic heart-failure signs, delaying recognition of the aortic murmur
Mild hs-troponin rise may be misread as NSTEMI rather than demand ischaemia from AS
Low-flow low-gradient severe AS can be missed if LVEF falls — dobutamine stress echo may be needed
Onset of exertional syncope in AS marks a sharp fall in survival and mandates expedited intervention
expectedMaiK: Exertional syncope plus angina and exertional dyspnoea with a slow-rising pulse, narrow pulse pressure and a late-peaking ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids is severe aortic stenosis until proven otherwise; confirm with transthoracic echocardiography and refer urgently to the Heart Team, factoring cirrhosis into procedural risk.
expectedNextQuestions: Were the syncopal/near-syncopal episodes reliably exertional?
Any preceding palpitations to suggest arrhythmia?
Progression of exertional dyspnoea and angina, and current functional class?
Child-Pugh/MELD status, varices, and bleeding/anticoagulation history relevant to intervention?
expectedInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography (peak velocity, mean gradient, aortic valve area, LVEF)
Serial high-sensitivity troponin to exclude ACS
Coronary angiography / CT coronary angiography as pre-intervention workup
Assessment of cirrhosis severity (Child-Pugh, MELD) for Heart Team risk stratification
regressionAssertions: Echocardiographic criteria (peak velocity >=4 m/s, mean gradient >=40 mmHg, AVA <1 cm2) must classify severe AS
Exertional syncope in severe AS must be flagged as high-risk requiring urgent Heart Team referral
Nitrates/vasodilators must be flagged as contraindicated in severe AS
Cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, coagulopathy) must be incorporated into procedural risk assessment
